newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl gets award for helping German Jews.
newsitem.headline: Kohl gets award for helping German Jews.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl received the German Jewish community's highest award on Thursday for helping to revive Jewish life in Germany since unification in 1990.

German Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis awarded Kohl the Leo Baeck prize and paid tribute to the German leader for his contribution towards reconciliation between Germans and Jews at a glittering ceremony in a Bonn hotel.

"The revival of Jewish religion, traditions and culture in Germany and his (Kohl's) efforts to promote Jewish immigration from the former Soviet Union after 1989 will forever be linked to his name," Bubis said.

Bubis said Kohl had expressly set out to boost the community that was virtually wiped out by the Nazi Holocaust and reduced further after World War Two when many survivors emigrated mainly to Israel or the United States.

"But you also deserve this prize because of your approach as a whole. You have never been one of those who said German history ended 50 years and we made a completely new start," Bubis said addressing Kohl.

Kohl joins a list of German and Jewish figures awarded the prize since it was instituted in 1957 in the memory of German Jewish Rabbi and community leader Leo Baeck. A Holocaust survivor, Baeck emigrated to the United States after the war. He died there in 1956.
Kohl recalled "the bitter words" of Baeck, who once exclaimed that after the Holocaust "Jewish life in Germany was over for good".
"We can all be grateful that this prediction has not come true," Kohl said.

Bubis said the chief two factors that contributed to the current revival of the Jewish community were German unification in 1990, which he attributed to Kohl's statesmanship, and the immigration of Jews from the former eastern bloc.
He praised also the German leader for his dedication to the promotion of Germany's and Europe's relations with Israel and for his support for the Middle East peace process.
In 1989 there were about 27,000 Jews living in West Germany in less than 60 communities many of which only existed on paper, according the Central Council of Jews in Germany.
Bubis said there were only about 400 Jews living in former communist East Germany.
But he said that from 1990 to 1996 the number of Jews doubled to 61,000 mainly due to an influx from Eastern Europe.

Since then a number of synagogues have been reopened, many of which were burnt down on "Kristallnacht" in a night of violence in November 1938, when Nazis mobs ransacked Jewish shops and businesses across Germany.
